name: Dynamic stretching warm-up

lead: A dynamic stretching warm-up uses controlled movements, such as lunges and leg swings, to raise blood flow and take joints through their range before training. The appearance payoff is indirect: better training sessions and fewer interruptions mean more consistent work on the physique.

Systematic reviews report that dynamic stretching before exercise produces small to moderate performance improvements, while long static stretches immediately beforehand can slightly lower performance.

paras: People do 5 to 10 minutes of light cardio and then movement drills that resemble the session, completed just before lifting or sport.
Low; ballistic bouncing may stress joints according to Wikipedia.

chain: Joints and muscles prepared; performance maintained
angle.text: Lifters use it before sessions to prepare for the work. The benefit to appearance comes through being able to train more.

lead: Dynamic stretching is movement-based stretching, such as lunges, leg swings and arm circles done with slow, controlled contraction, used in warm-ups to increase blood flow and prepare muscle for training.[1] It is the standard pre-lifting routine in many gyms and sports teams, and is usually paired with a few minutes of light cardio.[2]

For people building their physique the chain is: warm-up, better-prepared joints and muscles, more consistent and productive training sessions, and more muscle over time. A warm-up also helps lifters get into the movement patterns of the session ahead.[2]

A systematic review found dynamic stretching produced small to moderate performance improvements when done within minutes of activity, whereas static stretching of 60 seconds or more per muscle lowered performance immediately afterwards.[3] Another review reports a similar pattern, and notes that short static stretches below the point of discomfort often show no deficit.[4]

paras: Wikipedia describes dynamic stretching as slow, controlled active contraction, and ballistic stretching as a faster, bouncing variant that may cause joint damage.[1] Static stretching, by contrast, means holding a position at end range for a period of time.[1][2]

A typical warm-up, as described in general references, starts with a pulse raiser such as light jogging or cycling to lift heart rate and muscle temperature, followed by exercises that mimic the coming activity so the relevant muscles are activated.[2] Dynamic stretching drills (walking lunges, leg swings, hip circles, arm swings, trunk rotations) sit in the middle of that sequence.

Lifters and athletes use dynamic warm-ups before sessions to take joints through their working range before loading them. Forum training logs on T Nation, including long-running threads such as 'Just. Don't. Suck.', regularly mention mobility and thoracic or lat stretching before bench pressing or squatting as part of getting through a session comfortably.[5] The appearance payoff is indirect: sessions that start well, and fewer interruptions from joint or muscle problems, mean more total work on the physique.

A 2016 systematic review found dynamic stretching changed performance by about +1.3% on average, versus -3.7% for static stretching and -4.4% for PNF stretching, when testing happened immediately after stretching. It also found greater deficits with 60 seconds or more of static stretching per muscle than with shorter holds, and that no injury data were available for dynamic stretching. Range-of-motion gains from all stretching types typically lasted under 30 minutes.[3]

A 2011 review notes that stretch-induced deficits may be smaller or absent with short or low-intensity static stretching, and that dynamic stretching has shown either no effect or an improvement in later performance, especially when it lasts longer.[4] Wikipedia notes dynamic warm-ups have been linked with lower injury risk in volleyball, soccer and basketball.[1] The general warm-up article states that evidence for injury prevention in soccer is contradictory, and that some researchers think raising body temperature, rather than stretching, drives any protective effect.[2]
A 2023 meta-analysis of hamstring-injury prevention trials found that eccentric training reduced hamstring injury incidence by roughly 57% to 70%.[6]

A 2023 meta-analysis of 27 randomized trials with 606 participants compared dynamic and static stretching for hamstring flexibility and stiffness; it found no significant difference between them in acute range-of-motion gains.[7] A randomized trial in 40 professional football players with chronic low back pain and limited hip flexion tested an 8-week supervised dynamic stretching program of the hip flexors.[8] A 2024 meta-analysis of warm-ups in gymnasts compared static stretching, dynamic stretching and post-activation approaches on jump, balance and range-of-motion measures.[9]

The reviews above summarise trials of acute stretching effects on performance and range of motion.[3][4][7] Range-of-motion gains from stretching typically last under 30 minutes.[3] Additional trials have examined dynamic stretching in football players with back pain, in hamstring function with and without tissue flossing, and in high school soccer players for injury prevention.[8][10][11]

Dynamic stretching is low-impact. Wikipedia notes that faster ballistic bouncing may stress joints.[1] Warm-up length and intensity are commonly adjusted for cold environments, with longer warm-ups described for cold weather.[2]
